questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Three Dimensions
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072211/assets/f47c5a0a1cc62bc6aca913adea9f496e1a666017ec1cf5610b01535bf497af0d.png)

 

Consider the three-dimensional region of air shown above. All the surfaces of the region, except for the top one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes. The velocity field of the airflow is defined by 

$$
F(x,y,z)={z}^{2}\,i+2xy\,j+x{y}^{2}\,k.
$$

Current part:

$\text{div}\,F\,=$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =0+2x+0 \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
F(x,y,z)={z}^{2}\,i+2xy\,j+x{y}^{2}\,k.
$$

Earlier part 1:

$\text{div}\,F\,=$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        $2x$

Current part:

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072211/assets/dc432b01077dc153940a88689f398283c09ee2a9d3385f4619a2e4a12cfa9c10.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 4-x-y},
$$

where

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072211/assets/fcb2a304b7333a8ee3d2ae38c26b337fa4e486f0d33034b68982dc9f2cc0bb11.png)

Hence, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 4-x-y}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-y}dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-x-y}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4-x-y)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[(4-x)y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((4-x)-\frac{1}{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{7}{2}-x)\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{7x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

In part 1, we found that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-y}2x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented, use the divergence theorem to write down the integral that gives this rate.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $z$, treating $x$ and $y$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-y}2x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{4-x-y}2x\,dz]dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-x-y}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x(4-x-y)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(8x-2{x}^{2}-2xy)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(8x-2{x}^{2}-2xy)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(8x-2{x}^{2}-2xy)\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[8xy-2{x}^{2}y-x{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8x-2{x}^{2}-x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7x-2{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}7x-2{x}^{2}\,dx & ={[\frac{7{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{17}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our top (tilted) surface ${S}_{T}$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4-x-y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-x-y)=-1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨2xy,\,2z-{y}^{2},\,2y⟩{|}_{z=4-x-y} \\  & =⟨2xy,\,2(4-x-y)-{y}^{2},\,2y⟩ \\  & =⟨{{2xy}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{8-2x-2y-{y}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{2y}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{T}}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2xy)\cdot (-1)-(8-2x-2y-{y}^{2})\cdot (-1)+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-2x-{y}^{2}+8)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072211/assets/d0f9cb64d0ae1c3615df5a05c9f580bb9c74f6529efd732cfd83e1f4328ff8a3.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}(2xy-2x-{y}^{2}+8)\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2xy-2x-{y}^{2}+8\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$
